stem: A client with suspected lower-extremity peripheral artery disease has a resting ankle-brachial index (ABI) of 0.82. How should the nurse interpret this result?

options.A: It is within the normal ABI range and supports normal lower-extremity arterial perfusion
options.B: It primarily indicates impaired venous return rather than arterial disease
options.C: It is abnormal and supports reduced lower-extremity arterial perfusion consistent with peripheral artery disease
options.D: It indicates increased arterial perfusion because ankle pressure is lower than arm pressure

rationale: The American Heart Association identifies a resting ABI of 1.00 to 1.40 as normal and a value of 0.90 or lower as abnormal. In a client being evaluated for PAD, an ABI of 0.82 therefore supports reduced lower-extremity arterial perfusion and is consistent with PAD. C is correct.
educational_objective: Interpret an abnormal resting ankle-brachial index in a client evaluated for peripheral artery disease.
source_organization: American Heart Association / American College of Cardiology
source_document_title: 2024 Guideline for the Management of Lower Extremity Peripheral Artery Disease; How Is PAD Diagnosed?
source_locator: 2024 PAD guideline — resting ABI for PAD detection; AHA How Is PAD Diagnosed? — normal ABI 1.0–1.4, ≤0.90 abnormal, >1.40 noncompressible
source_claim_supported: Resting ABI is a standard PAD test; ABI ≤0.90 is abnormal and indicates reduced lower-extremity arterial perfusion in the appropriate clinical context.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential — diagnostic tests, laboratory/diagnostic values, and potential complications
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — ABI interpretation for PAD

source_original.stem: A nurse assists with an ankle-brachial index (ABI) measurement for a client with suspected peripheral artery disease, and the client assumes a lower-than-normal number would actually be a reassuring sign of good blood flow. The nurse understands that a low ABI value instead generally indicates:

options.A: Normal lower-extremity arterial perfusion because ankle pressure should normally be substantially lower than brachial pressure.
options.B: Venous insufficiency rather than arterial disease because ABI is designed primarily to assess venous return from the legs.
options.C: Reduced lower-extremity arterial perfusion, with an ABI below the normal range clinically supporting peripheral artery disease.
options.D: Increased arterial perfusion because a lower ankle-to-brachial pressure ratio indicates less resistance to blood flow.

source_original.rationale: The ankle-brachial index compares blood pressure in the ankle to blood pressure in the arm; a low ABI value (generally below about 0.9) indicates reduced blood flow to the lower extremities, consistent with peripheral artery disease, helping confirm the diagnosis and assess severity.
source_original.source_detail: 2024 PAD guideline, Section 3.1 Resting ABI: ≤0.90 abnormal; 0.91–0.99 borderline; 1.00–1.40 normal; >1.40 noncompressible. JACC 2024; DOI 10.1016/j.jacc.2024.02.013; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Converted the vague 'low ABI' item into interpretation of a concrete 0.82 value, used current official AHA/ACC sources, and avoided saying ABI alone confirms all PAD severity. Reduced difficulty from hard to medium while preserving Reduction of Risk Potential.

audit_findings.source_authority: 2024 AHA/ACC PAD guideline plus current AHA diagnostic page; NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.currentness: AHA PAD diagnostic page current in 2026 and 2024 guideline checked 2026-08-17.
audit_findings.claim_audit: AHA directly states normal ABI 1.0–1.4 and ≤0.90 abnormal; the guideline identifies resting ABI as a primary PAD detection test.

distractor_audit.B: ABI assesses arterial, not primarily venous, perfusion.
distractor_audit.D: A lower ankle-to-arm ratio indicates reduced, not increased, arterial perfusion.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: C is uniquely correct for ABI 0.82 in a client with suspected PAD.
audit_findings.cueing: Removed client misconception narrative and used a concrete value.
audit_findings.blueprint: Interpretation of a diagnostic vascular test fits Reduction of Risk Potential.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked current AHA thresholds and 2024 guideline; C remains uniquely correct.
